items.title: Screen for prior mania before starting an antidepressant
items.learning_objective: Before treating an apparent depressive episode, establish whether the lifetime course is unipolar or bipolar, because antidepressant monotherapy can be harmful in bipolar disorder.
items.tested_decision: The best next step before prescribing pharmacotherapy for a depressive episode with bipolar red flags.
items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to an outpatient clinic with 3 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia, and poor concentration. She has had two similar episodes since age 17. Her mother has bipolar I disorder. She recalls that an antidepressant started 2 years ago made her feel, for about a week, unusually energetic and talkative with a reduced need for sleep, after which it was stopped. She takes no medications now and denies current mania. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before starting pharmacotherapy?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before starting pharmacotherapy?

options.t: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and reassess in 4 weeks

trap.name: Antidepressant monotherapy in unrecognized bipolar
trap.note: Treating an apparent depression without ruling out bipolarity can precipitate a switch — the history must come first.

options.t: Take a structured history for prior manic or hypomanic episodes to clarify unipolar versus bipolar illness
Start a serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor because two prior episodes suggest recurrent unipolar depression

trap.name: Recurrence = unipolar
trap.note: Recurrent depressive episodes are common in bipolar disorder too; recurrence alone does not establish unipolarity.

options.t: Order thyroid studies and defer any diagnostic reassessment until results return

trap.name: Workup as a substitute for the interview
trap.note: Screening labs are reasonable, but they do not replace the mania history that changes the whole treatment plan.

items.why: The prior antidepressant-associated week of decreased need for sleep, increased energy, and pressured speech is a probable hypomanic/manic switch, and a first-degree relative has bipolar I — so 'antidepressant monotherapy in unrecognized bipolar' is the trap to avoid. 'Recurrence = unipolar' ignores that bipolar depression recurs, and a lab 'workup as a substitute for the interview' skips the decisive step. The history of past (hypo)mania is what distinguishes safe from harmful pharmacotherapy.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: The single most consequential branch point in treating a depressive presentation is unipolar versus bipolar, because antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can precipitate mania or mixed states and accelerate cycling. This patient has two bipolar red flags — early onset with a probable antidepressant-induced hypomanic episode (a week of decreased need for sleep, increased energy, talkativeness) and a first-degree relative with bipolar I. The correct next step is to take a careful history for lifetime manic/hypomanic episodes (DSM-5-TR criteria) before choosing a drug. If bipolarity is confirmed, first-line treatment is a mood stabilizer or a second-generation antipsychotic, not an antidepressant alone.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Starting an SSRI now is precisely the move that risks a manic switch in an undiagnosed bipolar patient; the diagnostic question must be resolved first.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Two prior episodes do not establish unipolar illness — bipolar depression is also recurrent, and this patient carries specific bipolar risk markers.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Thyroid studies are reasonable adjuncts but do not address the decisive unipolar-versus-bipolar question and should not delay the history.

items.pearl: Before any antidepressant, ask about past mania/hypomania — a first-degree bipolar relative and an antidepressant-associated 'high' are red flags for bipolar depression.
items.key_takeaway: Rule out bipolarity by history before starting an antidepressant for depression.
items.common_reasoning_error: Treating the presenting depression at face value without screening the longitudinal course for mania.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: If bipolar depression is confirmed, avoid antidepressant monotherapy; use a mood stabilizer or SGA per guideline.
items.evidence: Bipolar depression is distinguished from unipolar depression by a lifetime history of manic/hypomanic episodes; antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar disorder because of switch risk (DSM-5-TR; CANMAT/ISBD bipolar guideline).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Bipolar and depressive disorder criteria.

references.citation: Yatham LN, Kennedy SH, Parikh SV, et al. CANMAT and ISBD 2018 guidelines for the management of patients with bipolar disorder. Bipolar Disord. 2018;20(2):97-170.
references.note: Identifier from record; faculty to confirm exact version. Antidepressant-monotherapy caution in bipolar depression.

items.title: First-line treatment of adolescent major depression

blueprint.osteopathic_competency: Whole-person, family-inclusive treatment planning for an adolescent.

items.learning_objective: Select evidence-based first-line treatment for moderate adolescent major depressive disorder and attach appropriate safety monitoring.
items.tested_decision: The most appropriate initial treatment for a moderately depressed adolescent.
items.stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought by his mother to a pediatric clinic with 2 months of persistent sadness, loss of interest in soccer, declining grades, and social withdrawal. He has no manic history, no active suicidal ideation, and no prior treatment. His safety plan is in place and his mother is engaged. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.t: Paroxetine plus supportive check-ins in 8 weeks

trap.name: Wrong SSRI in adolescents
trap.note: Paroxetine has the least favorable benefit–risk in youth; fluoxetine has the strongest evidence base for adolescent depression.

options.t: Bupropion monotherapy

trap.name: Off-first-line antidepressant
trap.note: Bupropion is not a first-line agent for adolescent MDD; the SSRIs with pediatric evidence are.

options.t: Fluoxetine combined with cognitive behavioral therapy
Watchful waiting with no active treatment for 3 months

trap.name: Undertreating moderate depression
trap.note: Moderate, functionally impairing depression warrants active treatment, not months of passive observation.

items.why: For moderate adolescent MDD, the best-supported plan pairs an SSRI with the strongest pediatric evidence (fluoxetine) and CBT, with early monitoring for emergent suicidality. 'Wrong SSRI in adolescents' (paroxetine) and an 'off-first-line antidepressant' (bupropion) are the pharmacologic traps; 'undertreating moderate depression' with watchful waiting leaves impairing illness untreated.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Combination treatment with fluoxetine plus cognitive behavioral therapy has the best evidence for moderate-to-severe adolescent major depression, improving response over either alone. Fluoxetine and escitalopram are the SSRIs with pediatric approval, and fluoxetine has the largest trial base in this age group. Because antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal ideation/behavior in patients under 25, the plan must include close monitoring, especially in the first weeks and after dose changes, together with family engagement and a safety plan.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Paroxetine is specifically avoided in youth because of an unfavorable benefit–risk profile; it is not the SSRI of choice here.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Bupropion is not first-line for adolescent depression and lacks the pediatric evidence base the SSRIs have.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Watchful waiting is appropriate only for mild, brief presentations; this functionally impairing episode warrants active treatment.

items.pearl: Adolescent MDD: fluoxetine + CBT is the best-evidenced combination — and monitor for emergent suicidality early (boxed warning under age 25).
items.key_takeaway: Combine fluoxetine with CBT for moderate adolescent depression and monitor closely early in treatment.
items.common_reasoning_error: Choosing any antidepressant without recognizing that agent selection and suicidality monitoring differ in youth.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for suicidal ideation in patients under 25; monitor closely and involve the family.
items.evidence: Combined fluoxetine and CBT is first-line for moderate-to-severe adolescent MDD; antidepressants carry a boxed warning for suicidality in those under 25 (AACAP depression parameter; FDA SSRI labeling).

references.citation: American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP). Practice Parameter for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents With Depressive Disorders. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry. 2007;46(11):1503-1526.
references.note: Faculty to confirm current AACAP parameter/version.

references.citation: US Food and Drug Administration. Antidepressant medications: boxed warning on suicidality in patients under 25; fluoxetine prescribing information.
references.note: Faculty to confirm current label text via DailyMed/Drugs@FDA.

items.title: Schizophreniform vs schizophrenia — the duration criterion
items.exam_emphasis_note: Foundational DSM-5-TR duration-criterion discrimination in NBME diagnosis style.
items.learning_objective: Apply the DSM-5-TR duration thresholds that separate brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, and schizophrenia.
items.tested_decision: The most likely diagnosis given the total duration of continuous illness.
items.stem: A 20-year-old man is evaluated in clinic for 3 months of continuous delusions of persecution, auditory hallucinations, and disorganized speech, with a decline in self-care and school performance. There is no substance use, no mood episode, and a normal medical workup. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Brief psychotic disorder

trap.name: Ignoring the 1-month floor
trap.note: Brief psychotic disorder resolves within 1 month; 3 months of symptoms exceeds it.

options.t: Schizophrenia

trap.name: Overshooting the 6-month threshold
trap.note: Schizophrenia requires ≥6 months of continuous signs; at 3 months that threshold is not yet met.

options.t: Schizophreniform disorder
Schizoaffective disorder

trap.name: Diagnosing mood where there is none
trap.note: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with psychosis; none is described here.

items.why: Continuous psychosis of 3 months, with mood and substance/medical causes excluded, fits schizophreniform disorder (1–6 months). 'Ignoring the 1-month floor' overcalls brief psychotic disorder, 'overshooting the 6-month threshold' prematurely calls schizophrenia, and 'diagnosing mood where there is none' misreads schizoaffective disorder, which needs a concurrent mood episode.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: The schizophrenia-spectrum disorders are separated largely by duration once substance-induced and mood-related psychoses are excluded. Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but fully remits within 1 month; schizophreniform disorder spans 1 to 6 months; schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of continuous disturbance (including prodromal/residual signs) with at least 1 month of active symptoms. At 3 months with no mood episode and a negative medical/substance workup, this is schizophreniform disorder — a provisional diagnosis that converts to schizophrenia if signs persist beyond 6 months.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Brief psychotic disorder must remit within 1 month; 3 months rules it out.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Schizophrenia requires ≥6 months of continuous signs, which have not yet elapsed.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Schizoaffective disorder requires a concurrent major mood episode, which is absent here.

items.pearl: Psychosis duration: <1 month = brief psychotic; 1–6 months = schizophreniform; ≥6 months = schizophrenia (mood/substance excluded).
items.key_takeaway: 1–6 months of primary psychosis is schizophreniform disorder.
items.common_reasoning_error: Anchoring on symptom severity rather than the duration criterion that defines the specific diagnosis.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Schizophreniform is provisional; reassess at 6 months and confirm substance/medical causes remain excluded.
items.evidence: DSM-5-TR duration criteria: brief psychotic disorder <1 month; schizophreniform 1–6 months; schizophrenia ≥6 months with ≥1 month active symptoms.

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Schizophrenia-spectrum duration criteria.

items.title: Clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
items.learning_objective: Recognize treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials) and identify clozapine as the indicated next agent, understanding why.
items.tested_decision: The next pharmacologic step after two adequate failed antipsychotic trials.
items.stem: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia has completed two separate antipsychotic trials — risperidone and then olanzapine — each at an adequate dose for 6 weeks with documented adherence, yet he continues to have persistent hallucinations and functional impairment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next pharmacologic step?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next pharmacologic step?

options.t: Combine risperidone and olanzapine at full doses

trap.name: Antipsychotic polypharmacy reflex
trap.note: Routine two-antipsychotic combinations lack efficacy evidence and add side effects; they are not the indicated step for resistance.

options.t: Start clozapine with the required absolute neutrophil count monitoring
Add a benzodiazepine to control the psychosis

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines do not treat primary psychosis; they are not an antipsychotic strategy.

options.t: Try a third first-line second-generation antipsychotic before considering clozapine

trap.name: Delaying clozapine
trap.note: After two adequate failures the criterion for treatment resistance is met; further routine agents delay the one drug with proven superiority.

items.why: Two adequate antipsychotic trials have failed, meeting the definition of treatment-resistant schizophrenia, so clozapine (with ANC monitoring) is indicated. The 'antipsychotic polypharmacy reflex' and 'the reflexive benzodiazepine' are not evidence-based resistance strategies, and 'delaying clozapine' for a third ordinary agent withholds the only drug with demonstrated superiority in this setting.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as persistent symptoms despite two adequate trials (dose and duration) of different antipsychotics. Clozapine is the only agent with proven superior efficacy in this population and is the guideline-indicated next step, accepting mandatory absolute neutrophil count monitoring because of agranulocytosis risk. Neither antipsychotic combinations nor benzodiazepines have efficacy evidence for resistant psychosis, and adding a third routine antipsychotic simply delays effective treatment.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Antipsychotic polypharmacy is not supported for treatment resistance and increases adverse effects.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Benzodiazepines do not treat primary psychosis and are not an antipsychotic strategy.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: The two-failed-trial criterion for resistance is already met; a third routine agent delays clozapine without evidence of benefit.

items.pearl: Two adequate antipsychotic failures = treatment-resistant schizophrenia → clozapine (with ANC monitoring). Don't delay it.
items.key_takeaway: Clozapine is the indicated agent for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
items.common_reasoning_error: Cycling through additional ordinary antipsychotics or combinations instead of moving to clozapine once resistance is established.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Clozapine requires ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis and carries risks of myocarditis, seizures, metabolic effects, and severe constipation.
items.evidence: Clozapine is superior to other antipsychotics for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate failed trials (Kane et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988; APA Schizophrenia guideline 2020).

references.citation: Kane J, Honigfeld G, Singer J, Meltzer H. Clozapine for the treatment-resistant schizophrenic. A double-blind comparison with chlorpromazine. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 1988;45(9):789-796.
references.note: Foundational trial establishing clozapine efficacy in resistance.

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, 3rd ed. Washington, DC: APA; 2020.
references.note: Faculty to confirm guideline recommendation and clozapine-monitoring specifics.

tier2.q: What is the best reason clozapine is the correct choice here?

options.t: It is the only antipsychotic with demonstrated superior efficacy specifically in treatment-resistant schizophrenia
Combining two antipsychotics is generally more effective than any single agent
Benzodiazepines potentiate antipsychotic effect on hallucinations
A third second-generation antipsychotic is statistically likely to succeed where two failed

tier2.why: The rationale is efficacy in resistance specifically: clozapine uniquely outperforms other agents once two adequate trials have failed. The distractor rationales mirror the tier-1 traps — polypharmacy superiority, benzodiazepine potentiation, and the low-yield third routine agent — none of which is supported.

items.title: PTSD vs acute stress disorder — the 1-month line
items.exam_emphasis_note: DSM-5-TR criterion/duration discrimination in NBME diagnosis style.
items.learning_objective: Differentiate acute stress disorder from posttraumatic stress disorder by symptom duration after a qualifying trauma.
items.tested_decision: The most likely diagnosis given symptom duration after a traumatic event.
items.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to clinic 10 weeks after a serious motor-vehicle collision. Since the crash she has had intrusive memories and nightmares, avoids driving, feels persistently on edge and hypervigilant, and startles easily; these symptoms have continued throughout the interval and impair her work. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Acute stress disorder

trap.name: Missing the 1-month ceiling
trap.note: Acute stress disorder applies from 3 days to 1 month post-trauma; symptoms beyond 1 month point to PTSD.

options.t: Adjustment disorder with anxiety

trap.name: Downgrading trauma to a stressor
trap.note: A life-threatening event with re-experiencing/avoidance/hyperarousal defines a trauma disorder, not an adjustment disorder.

options.t: Generalized anxiety disorder

trap.name: Ignoring the traumatic anchor
trap.note: GAD is free-floating worry across domains, not trauma-cued re-experiencing and avoidance.

options.t: Posttraumatic stress disorder

items.why: Trauma-linked intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal persisting beyond 1 month is PTSD. 'Missing the 1-month ceiling' overcalls acute stress disorder, 'downgrading trauma to a stressor' misassigns adjustment disorder, and 'ignoring the traumatic anchor' misreads GAD, whose worry is not trauma-cued.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Acute stress disorder and PTSD share trauma-related intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions/mood, and arousal symptoms; they are distinguished by timing. Acute stress disorder is diagnosed from 3 days to 1 month after the event; when the full symptom picture persists beyond 1 month, the diagnosis is PTSD. At 10 weeks with continuous, impairing trauma symptoms, this is PTSD.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Acute stress disorder is time-limited to the first month; symptoms at 10 weeks exceed that window.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Adjustment disorder does not fit a Criterion-A trauma with the classic re-experiencing/avoidance/hyperarousal cluster.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: GAD is pervasive worry across life domains, not event-cued re-experiencing and avoidance.

items.pearl: Trauma symptoms 3 days–1 month = acute stress disorder; beyond 1 month = PTSD.
items.key_takeaway: Trauma-related symptoms lasting more than 1 month are PTSD.
items.common_reasoning_error: Defaulting to 'acute stress disorder' for any post-trauma presentation without checking duration.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Screen for co-occurring depression, substance use, and suicide risk in PTSD.
items.evidence: DSM-5-TR: acute stress disorder spans 3 days–1 month post-trauma; PTSD is diagnosed when symptoms persist beyond 1 month.

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Trauma- and stressor-related disorder criteria.

references.citation: US Department of Veterans Affairs / Department of Defense. VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Acute Stress Disorder.
references.note: Faculty to confirm current version.

items.title: First-line treatment of pediatric OCD
items.learning_objective: Identify cognitive behavioral therapy with exposure and response prevention as first-line for mild-to-moderate pediatric OCD.
items.tested_decision: The most appropriate initial treatment for a child with mild-to-moderate OCD.
items.stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to clinic because of 6 months of distressing intrusive fears of contamination and hours of daily hand-washing that she recognizes as excessive. Her functioning at home is affected but she attends school. There is no tic disorder and no recent streptococcal illness. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.t: Cognitive behavioral therapy with exposure and response prevention
Risperidone

trap.name: Antipsychotic for primary OCD
trap.note: Antipsychotics are not first-line for OCD; they are an augmentation option in resistant cases, not initial therapy in a child.

options.t: A benzodiazepine as needed for anxiety

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and are avoided as anxiety 'fixes,' especially in children.

options.t: Reassurance that compulsions are a normal childhood phase

trap.name: Normalizing impairing symptoms
trap.note: Hours of daily rituals with distress and impairment are not a normal phase and warrant treatment.

items.why: Mild-to-moderate pediatric OCD responds to CBT with exposure and response prevention as first-line, adding an SSRI (e.g., sertraline, fluoxetine) if needed. 'Antipsychotic for primary OCD' and 'the reflexive benzodiazepine' are pharmacologic missteps, and 'normalizing impairing symptoms' dismisses genuinely disabling rituals.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Cognitive behavioral therapy centered on exposure and response prevention is the first-line treatment for mild-to-moderate OCD in children and adolescents, with an SSRI added for more severe illness or partial response. Antipsychotics have a role only as augmentation in treatment-resistant OCD, benzodiazepines are ineffective for the disorder, and telling the family this is a normal phase both misdiagnoses and delays effective care.

explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Antipsychotics are an augmentation strategy in resistant OCD, not initial monotherapy in a child.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and are generally avoided in children for anxiety.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Impairing, distressing rituals for 6 months are pathological, not a developmental phase.

items.pearl: Pediatric OCD: start with CBT + exposure/response prevention; add an SSRI (sertraline/fluoxetine) if moderate–severe.
items.key_takeaway: ERP-based CBT is first-line for pediatric OCD.
items.common_reasoning_error: Reaching for medication (or dismissal) before offering the first-line behavioral therapy.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: If an SSRI is added, monitor for the under-25 suicidality boxed warning and start low.
items.evidence: CBT with exposure and response prevention is first-line for pediatric OCD, with SSRIs added for more severe illness (AACAP OCD parameter).

references.citation: American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP). Practice Parameter for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents With Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry. 2012;51(1):98-113.
references.note: Faculty to confirm current AACAP OCD parameter.

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: OCD diagnostic criteria.

items.title: Thiamine before glucose in the malnourished patient
items.exam_emphasis_note: Holistic, whole-person management of a malnourished patient with alcohol use — COMAT emergency/management flavor.

blueprint.osteopathic_competency: Recognizing nutritional and metabolic vulnerability as part of whole-person emergency care.

items.learning_objective: Prevent Wernicke encephalopathy by giving thiamine before or with glucose in a malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder.
items.tested_decision: The correct sequence of thiamine and glucose administration in a malnourished, altered patient.
items.stem: A disheveled 52-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use is brought to the emergency department confused and unsteady. He appears malnourished. A fingerstick glucose is 44 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.t: Administer thiamine together with (or before) intravenous dextrose
Administer intravenous dextrose alone and recheck the neurologic exam

trap.name: Glucose before thiamine
trap.note: Giving glucose without thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.

options.t: Give lorazepam for presumed alcohol withdrawal before anything else

trap.name: It's just withdrawal
trap.note: New confusion in alcohol use needs a real differential — hypoglycemia and Wernicke here — not a reflexive benzodiazepine.

options.t: Obtain a head CT before providing any treatment

trap.name: Imaging before resuscitation
trap.note: Correcting hypoglycemia and giving thiamine are immediate and should not wait on imaging.

items.why: In a malnourished patient with alcohol use, thiamine must accompany or precede dextrose because a glucose load can consume marginal thiamine stores and trigger Wernicke encephalopathy. 'Glucose before thiamine' is the classic error; 'it's just withdrawal' skips the differential; 'imaging before resuscitation' delays two time-critical, low-risk treatments.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Thiamine is a cofactor for glucose metabolism, and administering a carbohydrate load to a thiamine-depleted patient can acutely precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia). In a malnourished patient with alcohol use and hypoglycemia, the safe practice is to give thiamine together with — or before — dextrose, then continue evaluating for withdrawal and other causes. Both interventions are immediate and should not be delayed for imaging.

explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Dextrose without thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in a depleted patient.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Benzodiazepines treat withdrawal but do not address the hypoglycemia or thiamine deficiency driving this presentation.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Head CT may follow, but it must not delay correcting hypoglycemia and giving thiamine.

items.pearl: Malnourished + alcohol + needs glucose → give thiamine with or before dextrose to prevent Wernicke.
items.key_takeaway: Thiamine before (or with) glucose in the malnourished alcohol-using patient.
items.common_reasoning_error: Treating the low glucose in isolation and forgetting the thiamine dependency of glucose metabolism.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Do not withhold glucose in true hypoglycemia — give both; ensure adequate parenteral thiamine dosing per protocol.
items.evidence: Thiamine should be given before or with glucose in patients at risk of deficiency to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy (standard emergency/toxicology practice; DSM-5-TR substance-related disorders context).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Substance-related and alcohol use disorder context.

references.citation: Schuckit MA. Recognition and management of withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens). N Engl J Med. 2014;371(22):2109-2113.
references.note: Identifier from record; faculty to confirm. Thiamine/glucose and withdrawal management.

tier2.q: Why must thiamine be given before or together with the glucose?

options.t: Glucose metabolism consumes thiamine, so a carbohydrate load in a deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy
Thiamine itself raises the blood glucose and corrects the hypoglycemia
Dextrose blocks thiamine absorption from the gastrointestinal tract
Thiamine competitively antagonizes alcohol at its receptor

tier2.why: Thiamine is a cofactor for glucose metabolism, so giving glucose to a depleted patient can exhaust the last thiamine stores and precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. The distractor rationales invent pharmacology the mechanism does not support.

items.title: Opioid overdose — recognize and reverse
items.learning_objective: Recognize the opioid overdose toxidrome and select naloxone as the immediate reversal.
items.tested_decision: The immediate intervention for suspected opioid overdose with respiratory depression.
items.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department unresponsive. He has pinpoint pupils, a respiratory rate of 6 breaths per minute, and shallow breathing. A friend reports he uses heroin. After beginning airway support and oxygen, which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
items.lead_in: After beginning airway support and oxygen, which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.t: Flumazenil

trap.name: Wrong antidote
trap.note: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and can precipitate seizures; the toxidrome here is opioid.

options.t: Naloxone
Intravenous lorazepam

trap.name: Sedating a sedated patient
trap.note: A benzodiazepine would deepen respiratory depression in an opioid overdose.

options.t: Activated charcoal by mouth

trap.name: Charcoal in the obtunded patient
trap.note: Oral charcoal is contraindicated in an unprotected airway and does nothing for the acute respiratory depression.

items.why: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression and obtundation is the opioid toxidrome; naloxone is the reversal. The 'wrong antidote' flumazenil targets benzodiazepines, 'sedating a sedated patient' with lorazepam worsens hypoventilation, and 'charcoal in the obtunded patient' risks aspiration and does not treat the emergency.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: The triad of depressed consciousness, miosis, and respiratory depression is the opioid toxidrome; the life threat is hypoventilation. After airway and oxygen, naloxone — an opioid antagonist — reverses respiratory depression and can be repeated or titrated. Flumazenil is for benzodiazepine reversal and is hazardous here; benzodiazepines would worsen sedation; oral activated charcoal is contraindicated with an unprotected airway.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and may precipitate seizures.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: A benzodiazepine deepens the respiratory depression that is the immediate threat.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Activated charcoal is contraindicated in an obtunded patient with an unprotected airway.

items.pearl: Miosis + respiratory depression + obtundation = opioids → naloxone.
items.key_takeaway: Reverse opioid overdose with naloxone after airway/oxygen.
items.common_reasoning_error: Confusing antidotes (flumazenil for opioids) or reaching for a nonspecific sedative.

items.title: Anticholinergic delirium — deprescribe the cause
items.exam_emphasis_note: Whole-person deprescribing in an older adult — the drug list as the diagnosis; COMAT holistic flavor.

blueprint.osteopathic_competency: Holistic medication review and deprescribing as part of whole-person geriatric care.

items.learning_objective: Recognize medication-induced (anticholinergic) delirium in an older adult and identify deprescribing the offending agent as the key step.
items.tested_decision: The best next step for acute confusion temporally linked to a newly added anticholinergic.
items.stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to clinic by her daughter for 5 days of new confusion, worse in the evenings, with fluctuating attention. Ten days ago she was started on diphenhydramine nightly for sleep and oxybutynin for urinary urgency. Her vital signs are normal, she is afebrile, and a basic workup is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Start donepezil for a new major neurocognitive disorder

trap.name: Confused elder = dementia
trap.note: Days-long fluctuating confusion is delirium until proven otherwise, not a new dementia to treat with a cholinesterase inhibitor.

options.t: Start an antipsychotic to treat the confusion

trap.name: Medicating the symptom, not the cause
trap.note: Antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation; they do not fix a reversible drug-induced delirium and add anticholinergic burden if chosen poorly.

options.t: Add a scheduled benzodiazepine at night

trap.name: The reflexive benzodiazepine
trap.note: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium and add fall risk except in alcohol/sedative withdrawal.

options.t: Discontinue the diphenhydramine and oxybutynin and reassess

items.why: Acute fluctuating confusion beginning after two anticholinergics were added is anticholinergic delirium; removing the offending drugs is the treatment. 'Confused elder = dementia' misreads the tempo, 'medicating the symptom, not the cause' with an antipsychotic ignores the reversible driver, and 'the reflexive benzodiazepine' deepens delirium.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: New confusion with evening worsening and fluctuating attention over days is delirium, not dementia. In older adults, the medication list is frequently the cause: diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are potent anticholinergics that commonly precipitate delirium. The key step is to deprescribe the offending agents and reassess, alongside general delirium care. Cholinesterase inhibitors treat dementia (wrong diagnosis and tempo), antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation, and benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in withdrawal states.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Donepezil treats dementia; the acute fluctuating course here is delirium, and no dementia has been established.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Antipsychotics manage dangerous agitation but do not correct a reversible drug-induced delirium.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Benzodiazepines deepen delirium and increase falls except in alcohol/sedative withdrawal.

items.pearl: In older adults, the drug list is often the diagnosis — anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, oxybutynin) cause delirium; subtract before you add.
items.key_takeaway: Deprescribe the offending anticholinergics to treat drug-induced delirium.
items.common_reasoning_error: Labeling acute confusion as dementia and adding a new drug instead of removing the culprit.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Reserve antipsychotics for delirium with dangerous agitation; treat underlying causes and support orientation, sleep, and mobility.
items.evidence: Anticholinergic medications are a common reversible cause of delirium in older adults; management includes removing offending agents (delirium best-practice; Beers Criteria for potentially inappropriate anticholinergics).

references.citation: By the 2023 American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria Update Expert Panel. American Geriatrics Society 2023 updated AGS Beers Criteria for potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2023;71(7):2052-2081.
references.note: Faculty to confirm current Beers version; anticholinergic burden.

references.citation: Inouye SK. Delirium in older persons. N Engl J Med. 2006;354(11):1157-1165.

items.title: Dementia with Lewy bodies vs Alzheimer disease
items.learning_objective: Distinguish dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer disease and recognize antipsychotic sensitivity as a management-critical feature.
items.tested_decision: The most likely neurocognitive diagnosis given fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism.
items.stem: A 73-year-old man is evaluated for 1 year of progressive cognitive decline. His family reports his alertness fluctuates markedly from day to day, he has recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations of animals, and he has developed a shuffling gait with rigidity. His wife notes he acts out dreams during sleep. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Dementia with Lewy bodies
Alzheimer disease

trap.name: Defaulting to Alzheimer
trap.note: Early, prominent visual hallucinations, fluctuations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder point to Lewy body disease, not typical Alzheimer amnestic decline.

options.t: Vascular neurocognitive disorder

trap.name: Assuming stepwise vascular
trap.note: Vascular dementia classically shows stepwise decline and focal deficits/infarcts, not fluctuations with visual hallucinations and RBD.

options.t: Frontotemporal dementia

trap.name: Mislabeling as frontotemporal
trap.note: FTD leads with behavioral/personality change or language decline, not the visual-hallucination/parkinsonism/RBD triad.

items.why: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder are the core features of dementia with Lewy bodies. 'Defaulting to Alzheimer,' 'assuming stepwise vascular,' and 'mislabeling as frontotemporal' each ignore this specific constellation.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies is defined by core features of fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder. This is management-critical because patients with DLB have severe neuroleptic sensitivity — antipsychotics (especially first-generation) can cause life-threatening reactions — so recognizing DLB changes prescribing. Alzheimer disease presents with prominent early amnestic decline, vascular dementia with stepwise change and focal findings, and frontotemporal dementia with early behavioral or language change.

explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Alzheimer disease leads with amnestic decline; early visual hallucinations, fluctuations, and parkinsonism are atypical for it.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Vascular dementia classically shows stepwise decline with focal deficits, not this triad.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Frontotemporal dementia presents with behavioral/personality or language change first.

items.pearl: Fluctuations + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + REM sleep behavior disorder = Lewy body dementia — and beware antipsychotic sensitivity.
items.key_takeaway: The DLB core-feature constellation distinguishes it from Alzheimer disease.
items.common_reasoning_error: Calling any progressive dementia 'Alzheimer' and missing the DLB features that change management.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Avoid or minimize antipsychotics in DLB due to severe neuroleptic sensitivity; if unavoidable, use lowest-risk agents cautiously.
items.evidence: DLB core features are fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder, with characteristic neuroleptic sensitivity (McKeith DLB consortium criteria; DSM-5-TR).

references.citation: McKeith IG, Boeve BF, Dickson DW, et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology. 2017;89(1):88-100.
references.note: Identifier from record; faculty to confirm. Core clinical features.

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Neurocognitive disorder criteria.

items.title: Serotonin syndrome recognition and first step
items.exam_emphasis_note: Adverse-effect recognition and mechanism — NBME foundational-science flavor.
items.learning_objective: Recognize serotonin syndrome from its neuromuscular signature and identify stopping serotonergic agents plus supportive care as the first step.
items.tested_decision: The most likely diagnosis and immediate step for a hyperthermic, hyperreflexic patient on serotonergic drugs.
items.stem: A 30-year-old woman on a stable dose of sertraline is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after linezolid was started for an infection. She is agitated and diaphoretic with a temperature of 39.1°C, and her legs show inducible clonus and hyperreflexia that is greater in the lower extremities. Which of the following best describes her condition and the appropriate first step?
items.lead_in: Which of the following best describes her condition and the appropriate first step?

options.t: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; restart her antipsychotic slowly

trap.name: SS mislabeled as NMS
trap.note: NMS features lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia with dopamine antagonists; clonus and hyperreflexia after adding a serotonergic drug point to serotonin syndrome.

options.t: Anticholinergic toxicity; give physostigmine

trap.name: Wrong toxidrome
trap.note: Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry skin and absent bowel sounds, not diaphoresis with clonus.

options.t: Serotonin syndrome; stop all serotonergic agents and provide supportive care
Malignant hyperthermia; administer dantrolene as the primary treatment

trap.name: Anesthesia-only reflex
trap.note: Malignant hyperthermia follows volatile anesthetics/succinylcholine, not an SSRI–linezolid combination.

items.why: Rapid onset of hyperthermia, diaphoresis, inducible clonus, and lower-extremity–predominant hyperreflexia after adding linezolid (an MAO inhibitor) to sertraline is serotonin syndrome; the first step is to stop serotonergic agents and support the patient. 'SS mislabeled as NMS,' 'wrong toxidrome,' and the 'anesthesia-only reflex' each miss the neuromuscular signature and the drug trigger.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis marked by the triad of neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, often lower-extremity predominant), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, diaphoresis, tachycardia), and altered mental status, developing within hours of increasing serotonergic activity — here, adding linezolid (which has MAO-inhibitory activity) to sertraline. First steps are discontinuing all serotonergic agents and supportive care (cooling, IV fluids, benzodiazepines for agitation); cyproheptadine is a serotonin antagonist option in more severe cases. It is distinguished from NMS (rigidity/hyporeflexia, slower onset, dopamine antagonists), anticholinergic toxicity (dry, no clonus), and malignant hyperthermia (anesthetic trigger).

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: NMS causes lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia over days with dopamine antagonists — the opposite neuromuscular picture and trigger.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Anticholinergic toxicity is dry and clonus-free; physostigmine is inappropriate here.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anesthetics/succinylcholine, not this drug combination.

items.pearl: Clonus + hyperreflexia + hyperthermia after a new serotonergic drug = serotonin syndrome → stop the agents, support, consider cyproheptadine.
items.key_takeaway: Recognize serotonin syndrome by clonus/hyperreflexia and stop serotonergic agents first.
items.common_reasoning_error: Confusing serotonin syndrome with NMS and missing the neuromuscular and temporal clues.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Watch for hyperthermia-driven complications; benzodiazepines for agitation, aggressive cooling, and cyproheptadine for moderate-to-severe cases.
items.evidence: Serotonin syndrome presents with neuromuscular excitation, autonomic instability, and altered mental status after increased serotonergic activity; management is withdrawal of the agent and supportive care (Boyer & Shannon, NEJM 2005).

references.citation: Boyer EW, Shannon M. The serotonin syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2005;352(11):1112-1120.
references.note: Authoritative clinical review of serotonin syndrome.

tier2.q: What best explains why this is serotonin syndrome rather than neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

options.t: Onset within hours with clonus and hyperreflexia after adding a serotonergic agent reflects serotonergic neuromuscular excitation
Lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia developing over days after a dopamine antagonist
Dry skin, flushing, and urinary retention from muscarinic blockade
A ryanodine-receptor response to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine

tier2.why: The serotonergic trigger plus clonus and hyperreflexia over hours is the serotonin-syndrome signature; the distractor rationales are the mechanisms of the tier-1 traps — NMS, anticholinergic toxicity, and malignant hyperthermia.

items.title: Choose an antipsychotic by side-effect profile
items.exam_emphasis_note: Adverse-effect/foundational reasoning about agent selection — NBME flavor.
items.learning_objective: Select an antipsychotic by matching side-effect profile to patient risk factors rather than by drug recency.
items.tested_decision: Which antipsychotic to avoid in a patient with metabolic risk factors.
items.stem: A 40-year-old man with schizophrenia needs a maintenance antipsychotic. He has obesity, prediabetes, and dyslipidemia, and prioritizes avoiding further weight gain. He has no history of significant extrapyramidal symptoms. Which of the following agents is most important to avoid given his risk profile?
items.lead_in: Which of the following agents is most important to avoid given his risk profile?

options.t: Aripiprazole

trap.name: Avoiding the metabolically favorable agent
trap.note: Aripiprazole is among the more weight/metabolically neutral options — a reasonable choice here, not one to avoid.

options.t: Ziprasidone

trap.name: Discarding a low-metabolic option
trap.note: Ziprasidone is relatively weight-neutral (watch QTc); it is not the agent to avoid for metabolic risk.

options.t: Lurasidone

trap.name: Overlooking a weight-neutral choice
trap.note: Lurasidone is comparatively weight/metabolically neutral and would be reasonable here.

options.t: Olanzapine

items.why: Olanzapine carries the greatest weight gain and metabolic burden among these options, so it is the one to avoid in a patient with obesity, prediabetes, and dyslipidemia. Choosing by side-effect profile — not by 'newer = better' — is the point; aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone are comparatively metabolically favorable, so avoiding them would be the error.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Antipsychotic selection is driven by matching each agent's side-effect profile to the individual patient rather than by drug novelty. Olanzapine (like clozapine) has the highest liability for weight gain, dyslipidemia, and glucose dysregulation, making it the agent to avoid in someone with established metabolic risk. Aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone are relatively weight- and metabolically neutral and would be preferable. CATIE reinforced that agents differ mainly in tolerability, and that a first-generation comparator (perphenazine) performed comparably to several second-generation agents — so choose by side-effect profile, not recency.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Aripiprazole is metabolically favorable and a reasonable choice — not one to avoid.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Ziprasidone is relatively weight-neutral (monitor QTc); it is not the metabolic offender here.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Lurasidone is comparatively weight/metabolically neutral and would be appropriate.

items.pearl: Match the antipsychotic to the patient's side-effect risk — olanzapine/clozapine are the metabolic heavyweights to avoid in metabolic risk.
items.key_takeaway: Avoid olanzapine when metabolic risk is high; choose by side-effect profile.
items.common_reasoning_error: Selecting by 'newest/most effective on average' rather than by the individual's tolerability risks.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Whatever agent is chosen, monitor weight, waist, glucose/HbA1c, and lipids at baseline and on schedule.
items.evidence: Antipsychotics differ mainly in side-effect burden; olanzapine causes the most weight/metabolic effects, and CATIE showed efficacy comparable across several agents including a first-generation comparator (Lieberman et al., NEJM 2005).

references.citation: Lieberman JA, Stroup TS, McEvoy JP, et al. Effectiveness of antipsychotic drugs in patients with chronic schizophrenia. N Engl J Med. 2005;353(12):1209-1223.
references.note: CATIE. Comparator was perphenazine (a first-generation agent), NOT haloperidol; olanzapine most effective on all-cause discontinuation but greatest metabolic burden.

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, 3rd ed. Washington, DC: APA; 2020.
references.note: Faculty to confirm; metabolic monitoring recommendations.

items.title: Suicide risk — lethal-means counseling as the next step
items.learning_objective: Incorporate access to lethal means into suicide risk assessment and act on it with means-restriction counseling.
items.tested_decision: The best next step after identifying elevated suicide risk with access to a firearm.
items.stem: A 45-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department after telling his wife he 'can't go on.' He has major depression, recent job loss, and increasing hopelessness, and he reports thoughts of ending his life. On further history he mentions there is a handgun at home. He is calm and future-oriented about seeing his doctor next week. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Reassure the family and arrange routine outpatient follow-up because he is calm and future-oriented

trap.name: Face-value reassurance
trap.note: Calm demeanor and future plans do not offset stated ideation with access to a lethal means; reassurance is not a risk plan.

options.t: Counsel on restricting access to the firearm and other lethal means as part of the risk assessment and safety plan
Have him sign a no-suicide contract and discharge him

trap.name: No-suicide contract as safety
trap.note: No-suicide contracts do not reduce risk and are not a substitute for means safety and a collaborative safety plan.

options.t: Document that he denies a specific plan and conclude the risk is low

trap.name: Denies plan = low risk
trap.note: Absence of a stated plan does not make risk low when ideation, hopelessness, and lethal-means access are present.

items.why: Stated ideation with hopelessness and firearm access is an actionable risk that calls for lethal-means counseling within the assessment and safety plan. 'Face-value reassurance,' the 'no-suicide contract as safety,' and 'denies plan = low risk' each substitute a false reassurance for the one intervention with evidence — reducing access to lethal means.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Suicide risk assessment must include access to lethal means, and means restriction (especially firearms) is among the few interventions with evidence for reducing suicide deaths. The correct next step is collaborative lethal-means counseling — engaging the patient (and, with permission, family) to secure or remove the firearm — as part of a structured risk assessment and safety planning intervention, with disposition determined by overall risk under supervision. A calm affect, absence of a stated plan, or a no-suicide 'contract' does not lower risk and must not drive premature discharge.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Calm demeanor and future orientation do not neutralize active ideation with firearm access.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: No-suicide contracts are ineffective and are not a substitute for means safety and safety planning.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Denying a specific plan does not establish low risk given ideation, hopelessness, and lethal-means access.

items.pearl: Always ask about access to lethal means — firearm counseling/means restriction is a core, evidence-based part of the suicide safety plan.
items.key_takeaway: Act on lethal-means access with means-restriction counseling, not reassurance or a contract.
items.common_reasoning_error: Treating calm affect or a denied plan as evidence of low risk and skipping means safety.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Determine disposition from overall risk under supervision; a student never independently discharges a patient with active suicidal ideation.
items.evidence: Restricting access to lethal means reduces suicide; means-safety counseling and safety planning are core to suicide risk management (safety planning intervention; VA/DoD suicide-risk guideline).

references.citation: US Department of Veterans Affairs / Department of Defense. VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide.
references.note: Faculty to confirm current version; lethal-means counseling and safety planning.

references.citation: Stanley B, Brown GK. Safety Planning Intervention: A Brief Intervention to Mitigate Suicide Risk. Cogn Behav Pract. 2012;19(2):256-264.
references.note: Journal not indexed in PubMed; DOI to be confirmed by faculty.
