items.title: Agitation — verbal de-escalation first
items.learning_objective: Prioritize verbal de-escalation and staff support in managing agitation before coercive measures.
items.tested_decision: The best initial approach to an agitated but not yet dangerous patient.
items.stem: A 34-year-old man with psychosis is pacing and speaking loudly in the emergency department after a long wait. He is irritable but has not threatened anyone or become physically aggressive. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial approach?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.t: Verbally de-escalate while alerting staff and keeping a safe exit
Immediately place him in four-point physical restraints

trap.name: Restraint-first reflex
trap.note: Restraints are a last resort for imminent danger, not a first response to loud, non-violent agitation.

options.t: Give an intramuscular antipsychotic and benzodiazepine before any conversation

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Involuntary medication precedes de-escalation only when there is imminent danger; here, engage verbally first and offer voluntary options.

options.t: Leave him alone until he calms down on his own

trap.name: Disengagement
trap.note: Ignoring escalating agitation forfeits the chance to de-escalate and can allow the situation to worsen unmonitored.

items.why: For agitation without imminent danger, verbal de-escalation with staff support and a safe environment is first-line. The 'restraint-first reflex' and 'agitation = antipsychotic' jump to coercive measures reserved for imminent danger, and 'disengagement' abandons a de-escalation opportunity.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Best practice (Project BETA) treats agitation on a continuum: engage the patient verbally, build a collaborative relationship, and de-escalate, reserving involuntary medication and restraint for imminent danger to self or others. Offering to meet needs, giving space, and involving staff both improves outcomes and protects safety. A student's role is to help engage and to summon support early — not to independently restrain or forcibly medicate.

explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Physical restraint is a last resort for imminent danger, not an opening move for non-violent agitation.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Involuntary medication precedes verbal engagement only when danger is imminent; offer voluntary options first.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Disengaging forfeits de-escalation and leaves escalating agitation unmonitored.

items.pearl: Agitation without imminent danger → verbal de-escalation and staff support first; restraint/forced meds are last resorts.
items.key_takeaway: De-escalate verbally before coercive measures.
items.common_reasoning_error: Reaching for restraints or IM medication before attempting de-escalation.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Call for help early, ensure a safe exit, and escalate to medication/restraint only for imminent danger under supervision.
items.evidence: Verbal de-escalation is the first-line approach to agitation, with medication/restraint reserved for imminent danger (Richmond et al., Project BETA, West J Emerg Med 2012).

references.citation: Richmond JS, Berlin JS, Fishkind AB, et al. Verbal De-escalation of the Agitated Patient: Consensus Statement of the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry Project BETA De-escalation Workgroup. West J Emerg Med. 2012;13(1):17-25.
references.note: Consensus statement on verbal de-escalation.

items.title: Borderline personality disorder — staff splitting
items.learning_objective: Recognize splitting on an inpatient team and respond with consistent limits and team communication.
items.tested_decision: The best team response when a patient idealizes some staff and devalues others.
items.stem: A 27-year-old woman admitted after self-harm tells the night nurse that the day team 'doesn't care' and that only the night nurse truly understands her, and she asks the nurse to bend a unit rule 'just this once.' The team notices staff beginning to disagree sharply about her care. Which of the following is the most appropriate team response?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate team response?

options.t: Have the favored nurse grant the exception to maintain rapport

trap.name: Rewarding the split
trap.note: Special exceptions reinforce splitting and undermine the consistent structure the patient needs.

options.t: Confront her about being manipulative in a group meeting

trap.name: Punitive confrontation
trap.note: Shaming labels the behavior as bad intent and damages alliance; the goal is consistency and validation, not confrontation.

options.t: As a team, hold consistent limits while validating her distress
Transfer her care entirely to the favored nurse

trap.name: Institutionalizing the split
trap.note: Concentrating care in the idealized staff member entrenches the split and burns out that clinician.

items.why: Idealization/devaluation with staff conflict is splitting; the response is unified team communication and consistent limits held with validation. 'Rewarding the split,' 'punitive confrontation,' and 'institutionalizing the split' each either feed the dynamic or rupture the alliance.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Splitting — experiencing people as all-good or all-bad — commonly emerges in borderline personality disorder and can fracture treatment teams. The therapeutic response is for the team to communicate openly, agree on a consistent plan, and apply uniform limits while validating the patient's genuine distress. This provides the predictable structure that reduces crises. Granting exceptions, shaming the patient, or funneling care to the idealized staff member all reinforce the split or damage the alliance.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Bending rules for the idealized staff member rewards and perpetuates splitting.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Public confrontation shames the patient and harms the alliance without providing structure.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Concentrating care in the favored nurse entrenches the split and is unsustainable.

items.pearl: Splitting is managed by the team, not the individual — consistent limits + open team communication + validation.
items.key_takeaway: Meet splitting with unified team limits and validation.
items.common_reasoning_error: Personalizing the idealization/devaluation and responding individually rather than as a coordinated team.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Maintain safety monitoring for self-harm; limits are held supportively, not punitively.
items.evidence: Consistent limits and team communication are the recommended response to splitting in borderline personality disorder (DSM-5-TR; borderline PD management principles).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Borderline personality disorder features.

references.citation: Gunderson JG. Clinical practice. Borderline personality disorder. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(21):2037-2042.
references.note: Identifier from record; faculty to confirm. Management principles including team consistency.

items.title: Borderline personality disorder vs bipolar II
items.learning_objective: Distinguish borderline personality disorder from bipolar II by the character and triggers of mood instability.
items.tested_decision: The most likely diagnosis for rapid, interpersonally triggered mood shifts with chronic emptiness and self-harm.
items.stem: A 24-year-old woman reports mood that shifts within hours — often from calm to intense anger or despair — almost always after feeling rejected by a partner or friend. She describes chronic emptiness, a pattern of unstable intense relationships, and recurrent self-harm during these episodes. She has never had a distinct multi-day period of decreased need for sleep with sustained elevated, expansive mood and increased goal-directed activity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Bipolar I disorder

trap.name: Calling reactivity mania
trap.note: Bipolar I requires a sustained manic episode; hours-long, rejection-triggered shifts are not mania.

options.t: Borderline personality disorder
Cyclothymic disorder

trap.name: Mislabeling reactive shifts as cyclothymia
trap.note: Cyclothymia is ≥2 years of subsyndromal hypomanic and depressive periods, not minutes-to-hours interpersonally cued swings.

options.t: Bipolar II disorder

trap.name: Reactivity mistaken for hypomania
trap.note: Bipolar II needs discrete hypomanic episodes lasting ≥4 days with a sustained mood change; her shifts are brief and rejection-triggered.

items.why: Rapid, rejection-triggered mood shifts lasting hours, with chronic emptiness, unstable relationships, and self-harm, are the affective instability of borderline personality disorder, not discrete mood episodes. 'Calling reactivity mania,' 'mislabeling reactive shifts as cyclothymia,' and 'reactivity mistaken for hypomania' all misread interpersonally cued lability as an episodic mood disorder.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Borderline personality disorder features affective instability that is rapid (minutes to hours), reactive to interpersonal events (especially perceived rejection), and embedded in a pervasive pattern of unstable relationships, identity disturbance, chronic emptiness, impulsivity, and recurrent self-harm. Bipolar spectrum disorders instead require discrete, sustained mood episodes: bipolar I a manic episode, bipolar II a hypomanic episode of at least 4 days with a distinct change in functioning, and cyclothymia at least 2 years of fluctuating subsyndromal symptoms. The absence of any sustained episode and the interpersonal triggering point to borderline personality disorder.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Bipolar I requires a sustained manic episode, absent here.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Cyclothymia is a 2-year pattern of subsyndromal ups and downs, not brief reactive swings.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Bipolar II requires discrete hypomanic episodes of ≥4 days; her shifts are hours-long and rejection-cued.

items.pearl: Rapid, rejection-triggered mood swings + emptiness + unstable relationships + self-harm = borderline PD, not bipolar.
items.key_takeaway: Interpersonally reactive, hours-long lability points to borderline PD, not episodic bipolar illness.
items.common_reasoning_error: Equating 'mood swings' with bipolar disorder without checking episode duration and triggers.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Evidence-based psychotherapy (e.g., DBT) is first-line for borderline PD; avoid reflexive mood-stabilizer/polypharmacy and monitor self-harm risk.
items.evidence: Borderline personality disorder shows rapid, reactive affective instability distinct from the sustained episodes required for bipolar I/II and cyclothymia (DSM-5-TR).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Borderline PD and bipolar-spectrum criteria.

items.title: ADHD diagnosis in a school-age child
items.learning_objective: Apply the DSM-5-TR requirements for ADHD, including cross-situational impairment and onset before age 12.
items.tested_decision: The most likely diagnosis for inattentive/hyperactive symptoms present at home and school.
items.stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to clinic because for over a year he has trouble sustaining attention, is easily distracted, forgets and loses things, fidgets constantly, and interrupts others. His teacher reports the same behaviors disrupt the classroom, and his parents see them at home. He is meeting academic expectations only with significant support. There is no mood, psychotic, or major stressor history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Oppositional defiant disorder

trap.name: Confusing inattention with defiance
trap.note: ODD centers on angry/defiant, argumentative behavior toward authority, not the attention/hyperactivity pattern described.

options.t: Generalized anxiety disorder

trap.name: Anxiety mimicking inattention
trap.note: Anxiety can impair concentration, but there is no excessive worry here — the picture is cross-situational inattention/hyperactivity.

options.t: Normal developmental behavior for age

trap.name: Normalizing impairing symptoms
trap.note: Symptoms in two settings for over a year that impair functioning exceed normal variation.

options.t: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder

items.why: Persistent inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present in more than one setting for over a year, with onset before age 12 and functional impairment, meet ADHD criteria. 'Confusing inattention with defiance,' 'anxiety mimicking inattention,' and 'normalizing impairing symptoms' each ignore the cross-situational, impairing pattern.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: ADHD requires a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that is present in two or more settings (here home and school), began before age 12, has lasted at least 6 months, and impairs functioning, with symptoms not better explained by another disorder. This child fits that pattern. Oppositional defiant disorder is defined by angry/defiant behavior, anxiety by excessive worry, and normal development would not produce cross-situational impairment for over a year.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: ODD is about defiant, argumentative, vindictive behavior, not the core inattention/hyperactivity here.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: GAD could impair concentration but there is no pervasive worry; the pattern is ADHD.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Cross-situational, impairing symptoms for over a year exceed normal developmental variation.

items.pearl: ADHD = inattention/hyperactivity in ≥2 settings, onset before age 12, ≥6 months, with impairment.
items.key_takeaway: Cross-situational, early-onset, impairing inattention/hyperactivity is ADHD.
items.common_reasoning_error: Diagnosing from a single setting or conflating ADHD with defiance or anxiety.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: If treated, stimulants are first-line for school-age ADHD; screen cardiovascular history and monitor growth, sleep, and appetite.
items.evidence: DSM-5-TR ADHD criteria require symptoms in ≥2 settings, onset before age 12, ≥6 months' duration, and functional impairment (AACAP ADHD parameter).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: ADHD diagnostic criteria.

references.citation: Wolraich ML, Hagan JF, Allan C, et al. (AAP). Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Treatment of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children and Adolescents. Pediatrics. 2019;144(4):e20192528.
references.note: Faculty to confirm current AAP guideline version.

items.title: Oppositional defiant disorder vs conduct disorder
items.learning_objective: Distinguish oppositional defiant disorder from conduct disorder by whether the rights of others or major age-appropriate norms are violated.
items.tested_decision: The most likely diagnosis for defiant behavior without violation of others' basic rights.
items.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to clinic because for the past year he frequently loses his temper, argues with adults, refuses to follow rules, and deliberately annoys his siblings, often blaming them for his mistakes. He has not been physically cruel to people or animals, has not stolen or destroyed property, and has not been aggressive or deceitful beyond arguing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Conduct disorder

trap.name: Overcalling conduct disorder
trap.note: Conduct disorder requires violating others' basic rights or major norms — aggression, cruelty, theft, destruction — which are absent here.

options.t: Antisocial personality disorder

trap.name: Adult diagnosis in a child
trap.note: Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18.

options.t: Oppositional defiant disorder
Intermittent explosive disorder

trap.name: Mislabeling defiance as explosive aggression
trap.note: IED centers on recurrent impulsive aggressive outbursts out of proportion to provocation, not a pattern of argumentative defiance.

items.why: A year of angry, argumentative, defiant, and vindictive behavior without violating others' rights is oppositional defiant disorder. 'Overcalling conduct disorder' ignores the absence of aggression/theft/destruction, 'adult diagnosis in a child' misapplies antisocial personality disorder, and 'mislabeling defiance as explosive aggression' misreads intermittent explosive disorder.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Oppositional defiant disorder is a pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, and vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months, without the serious rights-violating conduct that defines conduct disorder (aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness/theft, serious rule violations). Antisocial personality disorder requires age 18 and a prior conduct-disorder history, and intermittent explosive disorder is defined by recurrent impulsive aggressive outbursts. The absence of rights violations makes ODD the best fit.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Conduct disorder requires violation of others' basic rights or major norms, which are absent.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Intermittent explosive disorder is defined by impulsive aggressive outbursts, not argumentative defiance.

items.pearl: ODD = defiance/anger without violating others' rights; conduct disorder = aggression, cruelty, theft, destruction.
items.key_takeaway: Defiance without rights violations is ODD, not conduct disorder.
items.common_reasoning_error: Escalating a defiant child straight to conduct disorder or an adult personality diagnosis.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Parent management training and school collaboration are first-line; assess for comorbid ADHD, anxiety, and maltreatment.
items.evidence: DSM-5-TR distinguishes ODD (defiant/angry behavior) from conduct disorder (violation of others' rights or major age-appropriate norms).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Disruptive, impulse-control, and conduct disorders criteria.

items.title: Anorexia nervosa — refeeding syndrome monitoring
items.learning_objective: Anticipate refeeding syndrome in severe anorexia nervosa and monitor/replete falling phosphate during nutritional rehabilitation.
items.tested_decision: The most important complication to monitor as nutrition is reintroduced in severe anorexia.
items.stem: An 18-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (very low body weight, bradycardia) is admitted for nutritional rehabilitation. As enteral feeding begins, which of the following laboratory changes is most important to monitor for and correct?
items.lead_in: Which of the following laboratory changes is most important to monitor for and correct?

options.t: Falling serum phosphate
Rising serum sodium from dehydration

trap.name: Fixating on sodium
trap.note: The hallmark and most dangerous refeeding electrolyte shift is hypophosphatemia, not hypernatremia.

options.t: Rising serum calcium

trap.name: Wrong electrolyte
trap.note: Hypercalcemia is not the defining refeeding abnormality; phosphate, potassium, and magnesium fall.

options.t: Falling blood urea nitrogen

trap.name: Irrelevant marker
trap.note: BUN trends are not the refeeding safety signal; phosphate is.

items.why: Reintroducing nutrition drives an insulin-mediated intracellular shift of phosphate (and potassium and magnesium), so falling phosphate is the key refeeding-syndrome signal to monitor and correct. 'Fixating on sodium,' 'wrong electrolyte,' and 'irrelevant marker' each miss hypophosphatemia as the danger.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate reintroduction after starvation triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, depleting already low stores. Hypophosphatemia is the hallmark and can cause cardiac and respiratory failure, arrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis, and death. Management is to advance calories cautiously, monitor electrolytes closely, and supplement phosphate (and potassium/magnesium and thiamine) as needed. Sodium, calcium, and BUN are not the defining safety signals.

explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Hypernatremia is not the hallmark of refeeding; hypophosphatemia is.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Calcium is not the defining refeeding abnormality.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: BUN trends do not signal refeeding risk; phosphate does.

items.pearl: Refeeding syndrome = falling phosphate (and K, Mg) as feeding starts — advance calories slowly and replete electrolytes.
items.key_takeaway: Monitor and correct falling phosphate during refeeding in anorexia nervosa.
items.common_reasoning_error: Feeding aggressively to restore weight without anticipating the intracellular electrolyte shift.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Start low and go slow with calories; supplement phosphate/potassium/magnesium/thiamine and monitor cardiac status on telemetry.
items.evidence: Refeeding syndrome is characterized by hypophosphatemia (and hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia) with cautious caloric advancement and electrolyte repletion (eating disorder refeeding guidance).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Feeding and eating disorders context.

references.citation: Mehanna HM, Moledina J, Travis J. Refeeding syndrome: what it is, and how to prevent and treat it. BMJ. 2008;336(7659):1495-1498.
references.note: Identifier from record; faculty to confirm. Refeeding pathophysiology and management.

items.title: Functional neurological symptom disorder — a rule-in diagnosis
items.exam_emphasis_note: Mind-body integration and positive rule-in signs — COMAT holistic/DO flavor.

comat.presentation: Psychiatric Illness due to Medical Condition/Somatic/Sleep-Wake

blueprint.osteopathic_competency: Integrating physical examination findings with psychological context in whole-person assessment.

items.learning_objective: Recognize functional neurological symptom (conversion) disorder as a rule-in diagnosis supported by positive examination signs, not a diagnosis of exclusion.
items.tested_decision: The most likely diagnosis when a positive Hoover sign demonstrates internal inconsistency of weakness.
items.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of right leg weakness that began after an acute psychosocial stressor. On examination, voluntary right hip extension appears absent when tested directly, but strong involuntary right hip extension is felt under her heel when she flexes the left hip against resistance (a positive Hoover sign). Reflexes, sensation, and imaging are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Malingering

trap.name: Assuming intentional feigning
trap.note: Functional symptoms are not consciously produced; malingering requires an external incentive and intentional deception, not evidence here.

options.t: Functional neurological symptom disorder
Acute ischemic stroke

trap.name: Forcing a structural lesion
trap.note: The positive Hoover sign demonstrates internal inconsistency incompatible with a fixed corticospinal lesion, and imaging is normal.

options.t: Somatic symptom disorder

trap.name: Confusing with somatic symptom disorder
trap.note: Somatic symptom disorder centers on distressing symptoms plus excessive thoughts/behaviors, not a neurological deficit incompatible with disease on exam.

items.why: A positive Hoover sign shows the weakness is internally inconsistent — extension returns involuntarily — which rules in functional neurological symptom disorder. 'Assuming intentional feigning' misattributes conscious deception, 'forcing a structural lesion' ignores the positive sign and normal imaging, and 'confusing with somatic symptom disorder' misclassifies a neurological-deficit presentation.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Functional neurological symptom disorder is a positive, rule-in diagnosis: clinical signs demonstrate that motor or sensory findings are internally inconsistent or incompatible with recognized neurological disease. The Hoover sign does this for leg weakness — voluntary hip extension seems absent on direct testing but returns involuntarily during contralateral hip flexion against resistance. This is not conscious feigning (which would be malingering or factitious disorder), not a structural lesion (imaging normal, sign positive), and not somatic symptom disorder (which is defined by distressing somatic symptoms with disproportionate thoughts/behaviors rather than an exam-incompatible deficit).

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Malingering requires intentional feigning for external gain; functional symptoms are not consciously produced.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: A positive Hoover sign and normal imaging are incompatible with a fixed corticospinal stroke.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Somatic symptom disorder involves distressing symptoms with excessive thoughts/behaviors, not an exam-incompatible neurological deficit.

items.pearl: Functional neurological disorder is ruled IN by positive signs (e.g., Hoover), not diagnosed by exclusion.
items.key_takeaway: A positive Hoover sign supports functional neurological symptom disorder.
items.common_reasoning_error: Treating functional disorders as diagnoses of exclusion or assuming the patient is feigning.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Communicate the diagnosis positively and non-stigmatizingly; still exclude comorbid neurological disease when clinically indicated.
items.evidence: Functional neurological symptom disorder is diagnosed by positive signs of internal inconsistency (e.g., Hoover sign) rather than exclusion (DSM-5-TR somatic symptom and related disorders).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Functional neurological symptom (conversion) disorder criteria; positive clinical signs.

items.title: Decisional capacity — refusal is not incapacity
items.exam_emphasis_note: Autonomy and whole-person, patient-centered care delivery — COMAT flavor.

blueprint.osteopathic_competency: Respecting patient autonomy within holistic, relationship-centered care.

items.learning_objective: Assess decisional capacity as four decision-specific abilities and recognize that disagreement alone does not establish incapacity.
items.tested_decision: The best next step when a patient refuses recommended treatment.
items.stem: A 58-year-old man admitted with a diabetic foot infection declines a recommended below-knee amputation. He is alert, has no psychotic symptoms, and states he understands he could die without surgery but wants to try antibiotics first because he has seen a relative recover that way. His care team is frustrated by his refusal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Declare him to lack capacity because he is refusing a life-saving operation

trap.name: Refusal = no capacity
trap.note: Capacity is decision-specific and assessed; a patient may make a risky choice and still have capacity.

options.t: Seek a court order to proceed with surgery over his objection

trap.name: Skipping to the courts
trap.note: Legal escalation is premature before a structured capacity assessment and a conversation about his reasoning.

options.t: Ask a family member to consent on his behalf

trap.name: Bypassing the capacitated patient
trap.note: Surrogate consent applies only when the patient lacks capacity; an apparently capacitated patient's own choice governs.

options.t: Assess his decision-making capacity for this specific treatment decision

items.why: The next step is a structured, decision-specific capacity assessment across the four abilities — understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and communicating a choice — because refusal alone is not incapacity. 'Refusal = no capacity,' 'skipping to the courts,' and 'bypassing the capacitated patient' all substitute frustration or shortcut for the required assessment.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Decision-making capacity is clinical, decision-specific, and defined by four abilities: to understand the relevant information, to appreciate how it applies to one's own situation, to reason with the information, and to communicate a choice. A patient who demonstrates all four may make a choice the team disagrees with and still retain capacity. Here the man articulates understanding and a coherent rationale, so the correct step is to complete a structured capacity assessment rather than override, litigate, or seek surrogate consent. Surrogate decision-making and legal escalation apply only if capacity is found lacking.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Refusing a recommended operation is not, by itself, evidence of incapacity; capacity must be assessed.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Court involvement is premature before a capacity assessment and a discussion of his reasoning.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Surrogate consent applies only when the patient lacks capacity, which has not been established.

items.pearl: Capacity = understand, appreciate, reason, express a choice — decision-specific; a risky choice is not the same as incapacity.
items.key_takeaway: Assess the four abilities for the specific decision before overriding a refusal.
items.common_reasoning_error: Inferring incapacity from disagreement with the recommended plan.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: If capacity is lacking, follow the surrogate/least-restrictive pathway; legal standards for competence vary by jurisdiction.
items.evidence: Capacity comprises understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and expressing a choice, and is decision-specific; disagreement does not equal incapacity (Appelbaum, NEJM 2007).

references.citation: Appelbaum PS. Clinical practice. Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment. N Engl J Med. 2007;357(18):1834-1840.
references.note: Standard framework for the four abilities of capacity.

items.title: Confidentiality vs duty to protect a third party
items.learning_objective: Balance patient confidentiality against a clinician's duty to protect an identifiable third party from a serious, imminent threat.
items.tested_decision: The best next step when a patient voices a specific, serious threat toward an identifiable person.
items.stem: During an outpatient visit, a 35-year-old man with escalating anger describes a specific, serious plan to harm a named coworker within days and has the means to do so. He asks you to keep everything he says confidential. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Maintain strict confidentiality because he explicitly requested it

trap.name: Confidentiality as absolute
trap.note: Confidentiality yields when there is a serious, imminent threat to an identifiable person; it is not absolute.

options.t: End the session and document the threat without any protective action

trap.name: Documentation instead of action
trap.note: Recording the threat does not discharge the duty to take reasonable protective steps.

options.t: Protect the identifiable third party and manage acute risk, per local law
Immediately call the police to arrest the patient as the only necessary action

trap.name: Single-channel response
trap.note: Protecting a threatened party may involve several steps (risk management, warning/protecting, sometimes hospitalization); reflexively narrowing to arrest is incomplete and jurisdiction-dependent.

items.why: A serious, imminent threat to an identifiable person triggers a duty to take reasonable protective steps while managing acute risk, within local law. 'Confidentiality as absolute' and 'documentation instead of action' fail to act, and the 'single-channel response' collapses a range of protective options into one jurisdiction-dependent action.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Patient confidentiality is a strong but not absolute duty; when a patient poses a serious, imminent risk of harm to an identifiable third party, clinicians have a duty to take reasonable steps to protect the potential victim. What that requires — warning the person, notifying law enforcement, hospitalizing the patient, or intensifying treatment — varies by jurisdiction and case, so the correct step is to manage the acute risk and take reasonable protective action consistent with local legal requirements, rather than either preserving confidentiality absolutely or reflexively defaulting to a single action.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: Confidentiality is overridden by a serious, imminent threat to an identifiable person.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Documenting the threat does not satisfy the duty to take protective action.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Arrest is only one possible step and is jurisdiction-dependent; protection may require several coordinated actions.

items.pearl: Serious, imminent threat to an identifiable person → duty to protect overrides confidentiality; the exact steps depend on jurisdiction.
items.key_takeaway: Take reasonable protective action for a credible, imminent threat, following local law.
items.common_reasoning_error: Treating confidentiality as absolute or assuming one uniform legal rule applies everywhere.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Duty-to-protect/warn statutes vary by jurisdiction; involve supervising clinicians and follow institutional and local legal policy.
items.evidence: Confidentiality yields to a duty to protect identifiable third parties from serious, imminent harm, with specific obligations varying by jurisdiction (professional ethics; jurisdiction-dependent duty-to-protect law).

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. The Principles of Medical Ethics With Annotations Especially Applicable to Psychiatry. Washington, DC: APA; 2013 (as amended).
references.note: Faculty to confirm current edition; confidentiality limits.

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Clinical risk-context reference; legal duty is jurisdiction-specific and out of DSM scope.

items.title: Family meeting — means safety, validate then act
items.exam_emphasis_note: Relationship-centered, family-inclusive care delivery — COMAT/holistic flavor and the clerkship's signature archetype.

blueprint.osteopathic_competency: Engaging family and social supports in whole-person safety planning.

items.learning_objective: Choose a family-facing response that validates first, then advances means safety with a concrete, verifiable step, staying within the student role.
items.tested_decision: The best thing to say to a worried parent when planning means safety for a depressed young adult.
items.stem: You are meeting with the mother of a 19-year-old man recently hospitalized for depression with suicidal ideation. She is tearful and says, 'I don't know how to keep him safe at home — am I supposed to watch him every second?' The team has recommended securing medications and removing firearm access. Before uncovering the options, consider the function of the best reply: it should validate her fear and then translate 'keep him safe' into a concrete, verifiable means-safety step she can actually do. Which of the following responses is best?
items.lead_in: Which of the following responses is best?

options.t: 'This is frightening, and you should not have to watch him every second. Let's make it concrete — today we lock up his medications and remove the firearm, and decide exactly who does each.'
'I understand you're scared, but most people who have suicidal thoughts never act on them, so I really wouldn't worry too much about it once he is back home with you.'

trap.name: Quoting statistics at families
trap.note: Reciting base rates minimizes her fear and replaces a concrete safety plan with reassurance.

options.t: 'The safest thing is for you to supervise him constantly — keep him in your sight at all times, and don't leave him alone even for a few minutes, day or night.'

trap.name: Making the family responsible
trap.note: Assigning impossible around-the-clock surveillance sets the family up to fail and is not an evidence-based safety step.

options.t: 'Let's try not to dwell on the frightening parts right now — he honestly seems so much better today that I really think he is going to be just fine at home.'

trap.name: Avoiding the topic
trap.note: Deflecting from safety forfeits the means-restriction conversation that actually reduces risk.

items.why: The best reply validates her fear, relieves the impossible expectation, and converts safety into a concrete, assignable means-restriction plan (lock medications, remove the firearm, decide who does each). 'Quoting statistics at families,' 'making the family responsible,' and 'avoiding the topic' each abandon the one intervention — means safety — that reduces risk.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: A strong relational answer validates before redirecting, keeps the family from an impossible role, and advances safety with a specific, verifiable action. Here that means acknowledging the fear, removing the '24/7 watch' expectation, and operationalizing means restriction — securing medications and removing firearm access — with clear ownership of each task. Reassuring statistics, demanding constant surveillance, or minimizing the risk all fail the function the moment requires and are named relational traps.

explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Quoting base rates minimizes the parent's fear and substitutes reassurance for a concrete plan.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Requiring constant supervision is impossible and shifts the treatment burden onto the family.
explanation_for_each_distractor.D: Avoiding the safety conversation forfeits the means-restriction step that reduces risk.

items.pearl: With families: validate first, lift the impossible expectation, then make means safety concrete and assignable.
items.key_takeaway: Validate, then translate 'keep him safe' into a specific means-restriction plan.
items.common_reasoning_error: Reassuring with statistics or offloading responsibility to the family instead of concrete means safety.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Means restriction (securing medications, removing firearms) is evidence-based; coordinate follow-up and keep the plan within the supervised team.
items.evidence: Effective family safety communication validates and then advances concrete means restriction; means safety reduces suicide risk (lethal-means counseling; family engagement principles).

references.citation: US Department of Veterans Affairs / Department of Defense. VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide.
references.note: Faculty to confirm version; lethal-means counseling with families.

references.citation: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR). Washington, DC: APA; 2022.
references.note: Depressive disorder and suicidality context.

items.title: Discharge transition — the plan the system can hold
items.learning_objective: Design a safe discharge transition that pairs a timely follow-up linkage with means safety, rather than treating a safety plan as clearance.
items.tested_decision: The most appropriate discharge step for a patient whose acute suicidality has improved.
items.stem: A 40-year-old woman hospitalized for a depressive episode with suicidal ideation has improved and is ready for discharge. She has a completed safety plan. The team is deciding what most reduces her risk in the vulnerable post-discharge period. Which of the following is the most appropriate discharge step?
items.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate discharge step?

options.t: Discharge with the completed safety plan alone, since she already has one in place

trap.name: Safety plan = discharge permission slip
trap.note: A safety plan is one component of risk management, not by itself evidence that outpatient follow-up and means safety are in place.

options.t: Give her a clinic phone number to call for an appointment whenever she feels ready

trap.name: Passive referral
trap.note: An open-ended 'call us' referral has poor follow-through; the post-discharge window needs an actively arranged, timely linkage.

options.t: Deliberately delay any follow-up for several weeks so she can settle in at home first

trap.name: Ignoring the high-risk window
trap.note: The days-to-weeks after discharge carry elevated suicide risk; follow-up should be early, not delayed.

options.t: Schedule follow-up within a few days, confirm means safety, and arrange a warm handoff

items.why: The post-discharge window is high-risk, so the safest transition pairs an actively arranged early follow-up with confirmed means safety and a warm handoff. 'Safety plan = discharge permission slip' and 'passive referral' overestimate what a plan or a phone number accomplishes, and 'ignoring the high-risk window' delays the very contact that protects her.
items.complete_correct_answer_explanation: Suicide risk is elevated in the days-to-weeks after psychiatric discharge, so a safe transition is more than a completed safety plan. Best practice is to arrange a timely follow-up appointment (ideally within a week), confirm means safety, and provide a warm handoff — direct communication with the receiving outpatient clinician — so the plan is one the system can actually hold. A safety plan alone, a passive 'call us' referral, or a deliberately delayed follow-up all leave the highest-risk period uncovered.

explanation_for_each_distractor.A: A safety plan is one part of risk management, not confirmation that follow-up and means safety are arranged.
explanation_for_each_distractor.B: Open-ended 'call when ready' referrals have poor follow-through during the vulnerable window.
explanation_for_each_distractor.C: Delaying follow-up leaves the highest-risk post-discharge period without contact.

items.pearl: Discharge safety = early, actively arranged follow-up + means safety + warm handoff — not the safety plan alone.
items.key_takeaway: Pair timely follow-up and means safety with a warm handoff at discharge.
items.common_reasoning_error: Treating a completed safety plan as clearance and under-arranging the post-discharge linkage.
items.management_or_safety_caveat: Post-discharge is a high-risk window; ensure timely contact, means safety, and communication with the outpatient team; a student does not independently determine discharge readiness.
items.evidence: The post-discharge period carries elevated suicide risk; timely follow-up, means safety, and care-transition linkage reduce risk (VA/DoD suicide-risk guideline; transitions-of-care evidence).

references.citation: US Department of Veterans Affairs / Department of Defense. VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide.
references.note: Faculty to confirm version; post-discharge follow-up and means safety.
